Apple is continuing to develop a new feature that will automatically lock the iPhone when it detects the device has been snatched from its owner. Here are the details.

Apple is still working on an iPhone anti-snatch auto-lock feature

9to5Mac first reported earlier this year that Apple is developing a new iPhone security feature that can automatically lock the phone when it detects the device has been grabbed from the user.

Although Apple has yet to officially announce this feature, new code found in iOS 27.2 beta 2 shows that the company is still actively working on it.

According to new code discovered by 9to5Mac today, this internally codenamed "AutoLock" feature can use the following signals to determine whether the iPhone may have been taken from its owner:

  • Sudden acceleration consistent with the phone being snatched;
  • A paired Apple Watch remaining unreachable for an extended period;
  • Loss of connection with a paired Apple Watch;
  • Extended loss of network connectivity;
  • The device remaining unlocked for longer than a certain period of time.

In addition, the new code includes some safeguards against false positives, such as successful biometric authentication, certain foreground app activities that could be mistaken for a snatch event, and a backoff mechanism that temporarily suppresses further auto-locks after multiple auto-lock events.

The code also shows that AutoLock uses a voting mechanism — signals suggesting a potential theft can request a lock, while safeguards such as biometrics, familiar locations, or certain app activities can veto that request.

These new details add to existing clues in the code, including a "stolen-device protection"-like location safeguard that takes into account whether the iPhone is in a location familiar to the user.

Notably, the feature remains in development and has not yet been enabled or made available to users in iOS 27.2 beta 2. Apple has instead enabled the underlying AutoLock service in the background but kept the actual lock-executing component switched off — likely to test the underlying workings without actually triggering an auto-lock.

This means that, for now, this new code only gives outsiders a glimpse of Apple's progress in developing the feature. Whether it ultimately ships, and when, still depends on Apple.
